Evidence and caveats →
Measurement record

Tested as: shipping on the channel's usual rhythm → first-28-day views vs off-rhythm uploads (the claim predicts this goes up)

The question put to the data: On this channel, do uploads that arrived on the channel's usual rhythm out-perform ones that broke it?

Exact arithmetic: Median first-28-day views for uploads arriving within half the channel's typical 48.0-day gap, minus the same for uploads that broke the rhythm.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up. One dot per channel — 60 earlier readings were superseded by a later re-measurement of the same channel and are not drawn.

What this does not tell you

Measured refinement — Median days between uploads per channel (40 most recent uploads)

Measured directly: the median channel uploads every 10 days (middle half 7-20.9). The claim is about KEEPING a rhythm, not about its length; this shows what rhythms the fleet actually runs, which is the range any "weekly" advice has to survive.

Window: 89 channels with 8+ dated uploads; gaps over the 40 most recent. Each dot is one channel's median; hover a dot for its name.

Where the claim came from
Find a good cadence. Become part of people, their patterns
Warning cadence
Cutting upload frequency to 'increase quality' only pays off when multiple substantive things actually change (length, production value, format); one small change is not enough to double per-video views and the trade fails.
Source: Mario Joos
Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so it stays a Warning on the strength of practitioner testimony. A failure mode is worth avoiding on good authority; it has simply never been put to our arithmetic. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Where the claim came from
make sure you have multiple things you're changing or you're planning to change, because if you're just doing one most of the times, that's not good enough to double your views.
Rejected cadence · Refuted by our data
weak Correlation The trigger and the outcome move together on the channels measured. That is a pattern, not a cause. held 11% of 37 measurements 19 channels
Upload at least weekly (every two weeks only for exceptional production value); gaps longer than a week cause viewer churn and hurt both short-term and long-term performance because you fall out of viewers' routines.
Source: Mario Joos

Not measurable by anything we currently compute

A failure mode is worth avoiding on good authority; it has simply never been put to our arithmetic. This claim IS measurable and has been written as a lever: a longer opening before the video gets going → share of viewers lost in the first 30 seconds, expected to go up. It is tested by asking: Do longer openings lose more of the room before the video gets going? No analysed channel has yet had enough data for that test to return a number — every probe stays silent below its minimum sample rather than reporting a figure that would look like evidence. It will be measured automatically on the next run that qualifies.

The retention chart reports only 100 data points (one per 1% of the video), so a 20-minute video has one sample every 12 seconds and short events like jokes or cuts cannot be attributed from the chart alone.

Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — which is exactly why it sits at Theory rather than higher — the rung means the cause and effect behind it has not been quantified. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Measured refinement — Sponsor-read bleed depth per channel (median over its census's sponsor-read drops; share of the audience present that left)

Measured directly: the median channel loses 13.4% of the audience present across its sponsor reads (middle half 11.3-17.8%). The census does not know which reads were cross-cut, so this is the fleet's mixed reality, not a test of the technique: reads on these channels sit inside the claim's 10-20% block-read band. A per-read cross-cut label is what would turn this into a calibration probe.

Window: 9 channels with 3+ sponsor-read drops in their census. Each dot is one channel's median; hover a dot for its name.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: We hold none of the three. Our knowledge base stores curves, flagged moments and transcripts-as-quotes, but no labelled sponsor spans and no structural classification of how a read was edited. Only 42 flagged moments across the whole 119-video cohort mention a sponsor at all, none of them labelled by read structure.

Caveat: This is testable in principle with our pipeline — the segment census in src/lib/analysis/segments.ts already clusters sponsor reads from transcript cues and measures bleed depth — but it would need a read-structure label added and enough labelled instances to compare. Nothing in the current store supports the 10-20% vs 2% contrast, in either direction.

Where the claim came from
you can sometimes go from a 10% loss or 20% loss all the way to a 2% loss if you intertwine cuts or cross cut

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: Only 11 of 57 stored formats reach 5+ scored evidence videos. 22 of 57 have all evidence from a single channel, so they fail the independence test outright. The formats that fail the bar are precisely the ones carrying the headline numbers: of the 16 formats reporting >=2x lift, 12 rest on <=3 examples and 6 are single-channel. Spearman(distinct channels, lift) = +0.10 — channel diversity buys essentially no lift, meaning a format's high number is not coming from breadth of evidence. And the thin high-lift formats do not survive their own evidence: dropping one instance takes the >=2x group from 2.31x to 1.82x.

Caveat: We can show that thin, single-creator evidence produces unstable lift estimates; we cannot show that a 5-example bar would have produced better-performing ideas, because no ideas were published under both rules. The specific number five is not itself validated — three independent channels would likely capture most of the gain.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: Removing one video — the single best instance — drops a format's median lift by 0.24x (mean 0.34x). For the 16 formats claiming >=2x lift, the median falls from 2.31x to 1.82x when the best instance is dropped. 30 of 57 formats sit on exactly 3 matches (the miner's minimum), and 22 of 57 draw all their evidence from ONE channel. Dispersion inside a format is enormous: 'Exposing Secrets In [Game]' spans 7.72x to 1.05x; 'Best Motorcycle Superlative' spans 104.5x to 0.96x; 'I Made a Cursed Machine' spans 24.8x to 0.41x. Spearman(evidence count, reported lift) = -0.15 — the highest-lift formats in our library are systematically the thinnest-evidenced ones, exactly the selection artifact the warning names. Separately, 28 of 98 within-channel repeat groups contain both a >=1.5x and a sub-1.0x instance of the same shape.

Caveat: This tests our own miner's output, so it demonstrates the failure mode is live in our pipeline rather than proving it holds universally. The lift figures are median-based, so a single-instance removal moving the median by 0.24x is partly a small-n artifact of the median itself — which is the same point the warning makes.

Measurement record

Tested as: making the subject a world-superlative version of a thing (surfaced via superlative titling) → first-28-day views (the claim predicts this goes up)

The question put to the data: Do titles escalating to a superlative earn more views than plain ones?

Exact arithmetic: Median first-28-day views for titles containing a superlative or scope claim minus the same for titles without one, scaled by the pooled median.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Signed toward the claim, so positive always means the claim’s own prediction showed up. One dot per channel — 46 earlier readings were superseded by a later re-measurement of the same channel and are not drawn.

Contradicted: Brief: superlative delta -0.06 (maker-builds, n=21), -0.01 (motorcycle, n=48), -0.05 (roblox, n=51) — negative in all three niches. My corpus check across 46 channels: WITH n=21 median 1.01x vs 1.00x (p=0.71); age-adjusted 0.98x vs 1.00x (p=0.52); 1 of 3 channels with >=2 matches came out ahead. Our own channels: n=4, median 0.75x. The library agrees: 'The World's Most ___' 1.09x, "World's Most ___ People" 0.98x, 'I Made the World's Most <SUPERLATIVE> <THING>' 0.84x — three of the four lowest-lift formats we have mined. Channel G' 'I built "the world's best speakers"' returned 0.75x against his own median.

Caveat: Title keywords are an imperfect stand-in for a genuinely superlative SUBJECT — a video can be about the world's largest thing without saying so in the title. Sample sizes for the tight regex are small (n=21 corpus, n=4 ours) even though three independent measurements agree on direction. The claim's premise (no direct competition) is not itself tested; only its performance consequence is.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Three videos exceed 20x. The largest, RevZilla's 'The Best Motorcycle Helmets of 2026' at 104.5x, is 249,328 lifetime views — below the median first-28d views of four of our six analysed channels (Channel F 988,269; Channel E 691,316; Channel G 453,746; Channel C 309,078) and barely above Channel A's 224,066. Adopting that 104x 'proven' idea on Channel F's channel would be a 75% view drop if it merely reproduced its source performance. The other two are HomeMadeModern's 24.8x = 812,751 views and April Wilkerson's 37.7x = 2,344,651 — three formally comparable scores spanning a 9x range in absolute reach.

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. The extreme scores are partly an artifact of thin per-channel sampling — RevZilla's collected median is only 2,385 views, which inflates the ratio — so this illustrates the claim rather than measuring the frequency of the failure. Views are not TAM; a small-channel outlier could still address a large addressable market that the source channel failed to reach. The specific '52x' figure is not testable.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does this channel's demand arrive PULLED (a viewer types a query — how-to, product research, education, urgent repair) or PUSHED (browse and suggested)? Cannell's claim is already tagged to education and Galloway's already excludes search-driven channels, so the two rules are compatible the moment neither is stated as universal — but Eves's is stated universally, and that is the repair the store needs. Our corpus offers indirect support for the split: the search-driven motorcycle niche is the one where long titles help (+0.07 at n=127) and where naming a specific machine produced 12.0% CTR against a 4.40% channel average (7470d720ee0b), while browse-driven roblox punishes long titles hard (0.72x, -0.28). Add a required trafficSource scope tag to every packaging claim; roughly a third of this slice is silently conditioned on it.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is creator feeling being used as a VETO or as a SELECTOR? The bias Gannett identifies runs in one direction — saturation exposure makes creators crave more novelty than their audience does, corroborated by Erik Bork twice over (1b71420b9852: inexperienced work over-indexes on being different and fails on the other six criteria; 0bb10fcb4588: audiences value newness less than creators and critics do, preferring a known type with one big new thing). So boredom is diagnostic and excitement is not: 'this bores me' is trustworthy because a predictable ending for the maker is a predictable ending for the audience, while 'this excites me' is exactly where the saturation bias lives. Scope the two claims as a veto rule and a selection prohibition and both survive intact.

Checked: Realized breadth buys nothing measurable: Spearman(evidence count, reported lift) = -0.15 across 57 formats, and 16 formats post >=2x median lift on only 2-7 realized instances. Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What is this channel's binding constraint — ACQUISITION or RETURN — and is the reviewed OBJECT the subscription proposition or is the creator? A gear channel whose viewers subscribe to hear about the next product is not harmed by object-led loyalty; a personality channel using reviews as filler is trading its return rate for upload cadence. The complementary format finding is already in the store (11d4f227f7ea): serialised formats invert the pattern exactly — highest return rate and highest AVD, no new-viewer acquisition — which means the two are a portfolio pair, not competing recommendations. Our corpus confirms the clickability half at scale in one niche: review-shaped patterns dominate the motorcycle format table (Motorcycle CarPlay Product Review 2.61x n=7, Provocative Take + Bike Review 2.29x n=3, Product Full Review 1.67x n=16). We hold no return-rate or subscriber-conversion data, so the cost half stays untested here.

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What is this channel's binding constraint — ACQUISITION or RETURN — and is the reviewed OBJECT the subscription proposition or is the creator? A gear channel whose viewers subscribe to hear about the next product is not harmed by object-led loyalty; a personality channel using reviews as filler is trading its return rate for upload cadence. The complementary format finding is already in the store (11d4f227f7ea): serialised formats invert the pattern exactly — highest return rate and highest AVD, no new-viewer acquisition — which means the two are a portfolio pair, not competing recommendations. Our corpus confirms the clickability half at scale in one niche: review-shaped patterns dominate the motorcycle format table (Motorcycle CarPlay Product Review 2.61x n=7, Provocative Take + Bike Review 2.29x n=3, Product Full Review 1.67x n=16). We hold no return-rate or subscriber-conversion data, so the cost half stays untested here.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Which layer are you generating at — a NEW FORMAT or a NEW EPISODE inside a proven one? Fixation is a risk only where the output is supposed to be structurally novel; where the output is deliberately a variant of a known structure, exposure is not contamination, it is the input. The operationally useful split: run the anti-fixation freeze at the format/premise layer, and run outlier study at the topic/variable layer — which is precisely Marcus Jones's own asymmetry (topics inside, formats outside) read one level up. Erik Bork (02de88eed921) marks the third position: once you have generated, WATCH the competitor's version rather than avoiding it, because the differences are what make yours viable. So the rule is sequenced, not opposed — the store currently holds three timestamps of one process as three competing doctrines.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the constraint INVISIBLE (a production limit that shapes what gets made — budget, crew, shooting days) or PACKAGED (a rule stated in the title that the viewer must accept before clicking)? The evidence divides cleanly on that line and on nothing else: every pro-constraint claim is about production, and every anti-constraint claim is about a constraint the audience can see. An invisible constraint costs the creator options and buys focus; a packaged constraint costs total addressable market and buys a promise. The dossier's own twist rule (e8765927f618) is the test for the second kind — a constraint earns its place only when it alters the decision, difficulty, evidence or payoff, and destroys the format when it is invisible, cheatable, or so tight the outcome is predetermined.

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the gate apply to the SUBJECT or to the FRAME? Thomas Brag's 'hide the vegetables' case (0f3a8d1320d9) is the resolution sitting unused in the store: the same Moldova footage failed as 'Spending a Day with a Grandpa in Eastern Europe' and worked as 'Traveling to the Worst Country in Europe'. The subject was unpackageable; a frame existed. So the defensible rule is 'kill an idea for which no FRAME can be found', not 'kill a mundane subject' — and the correct funnel step is a frame-search pass before the kill, which none of the five gate statements includes. The second discriminator is traffic source: the gate is a browse-competition rule, and a channel whose views arrive from an established subscriber relationship (Brag's own 417a2ab32d77 — no objectively great idea, only ideas great for a channel at a stage) faces a much weaker version of it.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is creator feeling being used as a VETO or as a SELECTOR? The bias Gannett identifies runs in one direction — saturation exposure makes creators crave more novelty than their audience does, corroborated by Erik Bork twice over (1b71420b9852: inexperienced work over-indexes on being different and fails on the other six criteria; 0bb10fcb4588: audiences value newness less than creators and critics do, preferring a known type with one big new thing). So boredom is diagnostic and excitement is not: 'this bores me' is trustworthy because a predictable ending for the maker is a predictable ending for the audience, while 'this excites me' is exactly where the saturation bias lives. Scope the two claims as a veto rule and a selection prohibition and both survive intact.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: The best-retention video never wins on views: it ranks 7/10 (Channel F), 22/30 (Channel C), 9/9 (Channel E), 22/30 (Channel A), 18/30 (Channel D), 9/10 (Channel G). Conversely the top-viewed video is usually the channel's WORST retainer: rank 10/10, 29/30, 9/9, 30/30, 26/30 — the sole exception is Channel G at 4/10. Concrete instance: Channel E's best retainer (35.0% at half) drew 412,394 views while its 7,242,999-view video held 19.9%. Channel C: best retainer 52.6% -> 270,791 views; top video 2,987,622 views at 21.0%.

Caveat: The specific 62.3% / 27,000 / 20M anecdote is unverifiable here — I confirmed the shape, not the story. Same reach-dilutes-retention confound as above: the top-viewed video may retain worst BECAUSE it reached a broad audience. The pattern is therefore strong evidence that high retention does not predict views, and weak evidence about what caused what.

What this does not tell you
  • The smallest group behind this is 10 videos. At that size a couple of unusual uploads can carry the whole result.
  • The effect is real in direction but small. It is not wrong, it is just not big enough to be worth building a decision on by itself.
  • It did NOT hold on Channel G, Channel A, Channel G, Channel A, Phoebe Taylor, The BlackVeil Files, The Mountain Maker, Tropical Russian, The Carpenters Daughter, Coffey Custom Builds, Isabella Demarko, Visual Thinker, Phoebe Taylor, The BlackVeil Files, The Mountain Maker, Channel G, Tropical Russian, The Carpenters Daughter, Coffey Custom Builds, Channel A, Isabella Demarko, Visual Thinker, Hannah's Happy Home. Those channels are the interesting ones: whatever they do differently is the missing context.
  • At least one reading could plausibly have come from chance (p = 0.90). The p-values here are a normal approximation, reported rather than used as a gate.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Of 15 features x 3 niches = 45 tests, 40 produce a median shift of <=0.05x and fail to reach p<0.05. Only two features move anything reliably: curiosity cues (2 of 3 niches, p=0.0018 and p=0.009) and named-thing specificity (2 of 3, p=0.006 and p=0.033). Everything else the packaging literature treats as a lever — numbers, listicles, question marks, capitalisation, superlatives, brackets, emoji, dollar signs, year tags — is flat.

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. I tested title micro-features; the claim's cited example is a THUMBNAIL micro-feature, which we cannot analyse at all (no pixel data). So this supports the general principle in an adjacent domain rather than verifying the specific finding. There is also a power argument to make honestly: with 20-50 videos per feature per niche these tests could not detect a real 5% effect, so 'noise' here means 'no effect large enough to matter at the sample sizes a channel actually has', which is arguably the practical claim anyway.

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is length a CAUSE or a PROXY? Our own corpus says it is a proxy whose sign flips by niche — 'title over 60 chars' scores 0.90x vs 1.00x in maker-builds and 0.72x vs 1.00x in roblox, but 1.04x vs 0.97x in motorcycle (n=127, the largest cell in the table). The discriminating question is therefore: does this niche's demand arrive by BROWSE or by SEARCH? In browse-driven niches the long title is a symptom of two crammed concepts (Brag's actual mechanism) and reads as noise at feed size; in spec-driven search niches the extra characters are the brand/model/year the viewer typed, so length correlates with matching rather than with confusion. Reframe both claims as 'one concept per title' (causal) and drop the character count entirely (non-causal).

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Niche-level rho: maker-builds +0.047 (n=330, p=0.40), motorcycle +0.128 (n=406, p=0.009), roblox +0.036 (n=378, p=0.48). Per-channel the sign is a coin flip: 21 of 42 channels positive, 21 negative; only 6 reach p<0.05 and they split both ways (Motovudu +0.71, MotoJitsu +0.55, TwoWheelObsession +0.54, William Osman +0.40 vs KreekCraft -0.66, Kat -0.49). Bucket medians run in OPPOSITE directions by niche: motorcycle rises monotonically (<30 chars 0.87x -> 70+ chars 1.11x) while roblox falls off a cliff at the top (60-69 chars 0.80x, 70+ 0.26x on n=3).

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. Outlier score is a views measure, not CTR — a length effect that lives purely in click-through with impressions compensating would be invisible here. Also, length is confounded with format: motorcycle's long titles are largely episodic travel series with a loyal returning audience, so 'longer works' there may be 'series work there'. The claim survives because no consistent direction exists, which is weaker evidence than a demonstrated null with tight confidence intervals.

Where the claim came from
Character count does not create relevance, clarity, or desire. Different surfaces truncate differently.

The store already contains the reconciling pattern and does not know it: Loewenstein via Will Storr (c016b1b0d050, 029b6ab5c85b) says curiosity is an inverted-U over knowledge — weakest at total mystery AND at full spoiler — and the same internal source's other formulation (b252abcc8b24) is 'state the setup concretely and withhold the RESULT' ('I spent seven months in the wilderness. Galloway is attacking zero-information titles; the internal cases all carry a heavy stated investment. The second discriminator is demand timing — the Sturgis title was chosen to capture live event search within days, where the named event supplies the concrete half that the phrasing omits.

Syllable counting is also a crude complexity proxy and does not capture jargon-versus-plain-English substitution, which is the claim's actual mechanism.

Checked: The distribution IS heavy-tailed but not as extreme as the claim implies. Across 38 channels the median top-outlier is 3.85x the channel median; only 4 of 38 channels have any video at >=10x and exactly 1 (RevZilla, 104.5x) reaches >=100x. Max-over-p10 spread runs 6x to 387x. Inside the analysed cohorts max/median is 2.0x-10.5x and median/p10 only 1.2x-2.1x.

Caveat: The claim is a causal counterfactual — what the SAME video would have done with a better title — and nothing in observational view data can test it. What I can say is that the outcome distribution has enough tail to make 10x possible on roughly 1 channel in 10 and 100x on roughly 1 in 38, so the claim's headline numbers describe rare events, not the typical upside. Corpus channels are sampled at 15-40 videos each, which truncates the true tail and understates the maximum.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What is the test FOR — ATTRIBUTION or CHOICE? A single-variable test answers 'what caused the lift' and needs everything else held constant; a shelf test answers 'which promise does a qualified viewer prefer against real competitors' and is worthless unless the options are genuinely distinct. They are also different instruments on different subjects: the shelf test is a preference test run on humans before filming, the A/B is an inference test run on the platform after publishing, and the dossier's warning about sequential testing (confounding audience, time, competition, seasonality, momentum) applies only to the second. Note that most of the store's repackaging advice — post-launch thumbnail swaps at 3a914075eefa, d56353b68dce, 49aa550ff948 — is sequential by construction and therefore sits inside the invalidity the dossier names, which nothing in the store currently acknowledges.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What is the test FOR — ATTRIBUTION or CHOICE? A single-variable test answers 'what caused the lift' and needs everything else held constant; a shelf test answers 'which promise does a qualified viewer prefer against real competitors' and is worthless unless the options are genuinely distinct. They are also different instruments on different subjects: the shelf test is a preference test run on humans before filming, the A/B is an inference test run on the platform after publishing, and the dossier's warning about sequential testing (confounding audience, time, competition, seasonality, momentum) applies only to the second. Note that most of the store's repackaging advice — post-launch thumbnail swaps at 3a914075eefa, d56353b68dce, 49aa550ff948 — is sequential by construction and therefore sits inside the invalidity the dossier names, which nothing in the store currently acknowledges.

Measurement record

Tested as: the first 30 seconds of a long-form video → share of viewers gone by 0:30, measured against the 35.1% the claim asserts (the claim predicts this goes differs)

The question put to the data: Does the median share of viewers gone by 0:30 on this channel land near the 35.1% the first-30-seconds Law asserts?

Exact arithmetic: Channel median over videos of (1 - audience share still watching at 0:30) x 100, from the stored curve. Asserted 35.1; effect = (measured - asserted) / asserted.

Each dot is one channel. Filled green held in the direction the claim predicts; hollow red did not. The dashed line is the threshold — an effect smaller than that is real in direction but too small to build a decision on. Measured refinement — Share of viewers gone by 0:30, per channel (median over its analysed videos)

Measured directly: the median channel has lost 35.2% of viewers by 0:30 (middle half of channels: 29.3-37.5%), and 44.6% by 1:00. A precise re-signing would say "roughly 35% are gone by 0:30, 45% by 1:00" — the claim's 30% sits inside what the curves show — imprecise rather than wrong. Note: the probe this claim was once bound to tested something else entirely (whether intro hold correlates with views) — its 7%-held record never measured the claim's own number, and that binding was removed by adjudication on 2026-09-01.

Window: 19 channels with 8+ usable curves; every analysed video, not a recent-window slice. Each dot is one channel's median; hover a dot for its name.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Supported: By 30s only 8 of 119 videos had lost 30%; by 60s 100 of 119 had; by 120s 117 of 119 had. Median retention: 77.5% at 30s, 61.6% at 60s, 54.1% at 120s. So the 30% threshold is crossed inside the 30-60s window for the large majority. Per channel at 60s: Channel C 30/30, Channel D 30/30, Channel F 10/10, Channel G 10/10, Channel E 6/9, Channel A 14/30. Median loss by window confirms the shape: 0-15s loses 6.5-9.4%, 15-30s loses 0-19.1%, 30-60s loses 9.7-24.9%.

Caveat: Channel A (Roblox gaming, 19-min median) is a genuine partial exception — fewer than half its videos cross 30% loss by 60s, and it needs ~120s. Channel E (52-min median) loses almost nothing between 15s and 30s (0.0% median) but then drops 24.9% in the 30-60s band, so the window shifts with runtime. The claim's diagnostic prescription is sound; the word 'always' is not.

Where the claim came from
Go back and do it again at the spot where you lost the first 30% of your viewers. It's usually in the first 30 to 60s of the video. Figure out what triggered this drop so you can see how to adjust based on the data.
Law retention · earlier check spanned 7 channels
The standard fix for weak retention — cut the video shorter — is the wrong remedy; a retention problem in the back half is a setup problem in the opening, so the fix is better setup, not less runtime.
Source: Hayden Hillier-Smith
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the surface LOOP-SCORED (short-form, where completion and rewatch drive redistribution and the final second gates the loop) or watch-time-scored long-form? And is the trim removing a specifically DEAD trailing second, or removing runtime generally? Restated: (a) on short-form, trimming dead trailing frames is a direct lever on the loop metric; (b) on long-form, runtime is not the constraint — our own data has the longer half of the catalogue beating the shorter half on median first-28d views for 6 of 7 channels.

Reviewed by the team’s strategist

Yes, this tends to be true. Story elements that grip the viewer to keep watching in order to find out more is extremely important Decomposed into 2 atomic claims by our strategist (directed in chat 2026-09-02, executed by Claude) (2026-09-02).

Supported: The longer half beat the shorter half on median views in 6 of 7 channels (Channel C 321,662 vs 291,465; Channel D 65,205 vs 48,143; Channel A 251,961 vs 218,645; Channel F 1,012,676 vs 963,861; Channel B 287,063 vs 207,873; Channel G 485,039 vs 367,785). Channel E is the sole exception (691,316 vs 863,878). Pooled within-channel rho(duration, views) = +0.23, and rho(duration, AVD-seconds) = +0.69 to +0.85 in every channel — so shortening would directly destroy watch-time seconds while, in these channels, moving views the wrong way.

Caveat: Strictly this refutes only the remedy's premise (that shorter is better), not the claim's positive diagnosis (that the back-half problem originates in the opening) — that half is a causal story we cannot test without an edit experiment. Duration is also confounded with format: a channel's longest videos are often its most ambitious builds, which may attract more views for reasons unrelated to length. Channel E, the longest-form channel at 52-min median, is the one where longer loses.

Where the claim came from
if you have an act free problem, you have an act One problem. So what is our Act One problem? The common misconception of retention is to make it shorter. Instead, we need to tell it better.
Law retention · earlier check spanned 6 channels
A single video's retention spike is not evidence of enjoyment — it can be a rewatch, a share, a skip target, a surprising result, or a dense explanation, so the behaviour before and after the spike must be inspected before acting on it.
Source: idea-engine research dossier
Reviewed by the team’s strategist

Correct, context is highly important in any matter Decomposed into 2 atomic claims by our strategist (directed in chat 2026-09-02, executed by Claude) (2026-09-02).

Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so its Law standing rests on a human sign-off and earlier manual checks, NOT on the measurement ledger. Treat it as the team's settled judgement rather than a measured result. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: 37.8% of rises collapse within two samples (not sustained), and 25.1% sit immediately after a comparable drop — evidence about the moment BEFORE them, not the moment they mark. Only 45.0% survive both checks. Per channel the misread rate ranges from 20% (Channel C) to 90% (Channel A).

Caveat: Identical caveats to the previous verdict: curve-shape inference only, threshold-sensitive percentages. This also cannot distinguish among the claim's specific enumerated causes (rewatch vs share vs skip target vs dense explanation) — it only establishes that a face-value reading is wrong often enough to require the inspection step.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: Of 756 rises, only 62.2% (470) were still held two samples later, and 25.1% (190) were preceded by a comparable drop. Only 45.0% (340) pass BOTH tests as genuine replay candidates — meaning a naive 'a spike is a loved moment' reading would misclassify roughly 55% of them. The discriminator also separates channels sharply: sustained-rise share runs Channel C 79.6%, Channel G 76.7%, Channel E 73.9%, Channel D 61.7%, Channel F 58.6%, Channel A 9.9%.

Caveat: Both discriminators are inferences from curve shape, not observations of viewer behaviour — we never see a scrub event. The 2%/3-sample thresholds are ours and the exact percentages move with them. Channel A's 9.9% is extreme enough to suggest its short Roblox videos generate noisier curves rather than genuinely different behaviour. What is robust across all six channels is that a large minority-to-majority of rises fail at least one check, so the warning is doing real work rather than describing an edge case.

Where the claim came from
A peak caused only by viewers skipping to a timestamp is not automatically a good premise; confirm whether viewers continue watching afterward.
Law retention · earlier check spanned 6 channels
A universal average-percentage-viewed target is invalid because a high retention percentage can coexist with low demand — retention must be read as a curve against the channel's own comparable videos, not against a benchmark number.
Source: idea-engine research dossier
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply at different channel sizes. The question that separates them:

What is the video's RUNTIME and format, and is the 60% figure a distribution gate or a descriptive correlate of a specific challenge-entertainment format at ~10-15 minutes? A 60% APV on a 12-minute challenge video and on a 52-minute build video are entirely different demands on the viewer. Restated: (a) within one channel at one roughly fixed length and format, a rising APV is a real improvement signal; (b) no APV number is a cross-channel or cross-length gate on distribution.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: Within every channel the higher-APV videos are the lower-view ones (pooled rho = -0.54, negative 6/6, surviving a duration control at -0.51). Absolute APV levels differ enormously between healthy channels: median APV Channel C 48.3%, Channel A 42.3%, Channel G 42.9%, Channel F 40.0%, Channel E 32.5%, Channel D 31.2% — while median first-28d views run from 54,012 (Channel D) to 988,269 (Channel F), i.e. the channel with the LOWEST APV is not the weakest performer and the ordering of APV does not track the ordering of views.

Caveat: Cross-channel APV comparison is confounded by niche and by video length (median durations 17-52 min). The within-channel negative correlation is the stronger leg; it is still correlational, and the audience-widening mechanism could be what produces it. Either way the practical conclusion — do not read a fixed APV number as a quality grade — holds.

Where the claim came from
Video length, audience, traffic source, and promise change the meaning of average percentage viewed. A high percentage can coexist with low demand.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: The first minute accounts for a median 52-57% of a video's ENTIRE audience loss in 5 of 6 channels (Channel C 56.1%, Channel F 57.4%, Channel G 56.2%, Channel D 53.8%, Channel E 52.1%); Channel A is lower at 39.5%. rho(retention@60s, APV) is positive in 6/6 channels (+0.12 to +0.92). rho(retention@60s, AVD-seconds) is positive in 4/6 (up to +0.90) but negative for Channel F (-0.09) and weak for Channel A (+0.22).

Caveat: The arithmetic core is a tautology and needs no data. What the data adds is the magnitude — over half of all loss really is pre-60s — which does justify heavy attention there for AVD purposes. But the onward inference to reach fails in this dataset: rho(retention@30s, first-28d views) is +0.06 pooled and flips sign across channels (-0.37 to +0.68). So first-minute work buys AVD, and we have no evidence it buys views. The '25% of production time' allocation is a judgement call the data cannot price.

Where the claim came from
we spend probably 25% of our time on the first minute of the video because if you look at retention graphs, a lot of times I'll have a steep drop up in the beginning. And any viewer that drops off in the first minute is a viewer that can't make it to the end of the video

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: rho(duration, APV) is negative in 5 of 6 channels: Channel A -0.47, Channel F -0.52, Channel C -0.33, Channel E -0.30, Channel D -0.18; Channel G is the exception at +0.12. Caveat: Only the premise is tested. The claim's operative half — that when BOTH rise in the same window it is the signature of genuine improvement and licenses lengthening — requires a time series of the same channel before and after an intervention, which we do not hold. Channel G' positive duration-APV sign (n=10) is a reminder the inverse relation is a tendency, not a law.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. The measured record above is what this claim's standing now rests on.

Supported: The largest ABSOLUTE per-sample drop falls inside the first 5% of runtime for 116 of 119 videos (97%). The largest HAZARD RATE falls in the first 5% for 89 of 119 (75%), with the runner-up bucket being the final 5% (9 videos). Median hazard by band is monotone away from the opening: 1-5% band 7.0-13.1% per sample, 6-15% band 1.1-2.4%, 16-30% band 0.4-1.1%.

Caveat: 'First 5% of runtime' is 60-155 seconds on these videos, not 'the first frame'. Our resolution cannot distinguish frame 1 from second 30, so what is confirmed is that the opening BLOCK carries by far the biggest single loss — the claim's prescriptive half (that the first frame must deliver the thumbnail's promise) is untestable here since we do not analyse thumbnails or frames.

as soon as people click on it, the first frame and the first few seconds are so important because that's where 99% of YouTubers have the largest drop off, right? ... We deliver what's clicked on uh by giving some delivery on expectations one and also uh immediately addressing any interest gap uh to a certain degree. not the entire thing.

Warning retention
There is no correct fixed intro length: the opening must confirm the click, qualify the conditions, and begin movement, and complex ideas legitimately need more context than simple ones.
Source: idea-engine research dossier
Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so it stays a Warning on the strength of practitioner testimony. A failure mode is worth avoiding on good authority; it has simply never been put to our arithmetic. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Where the claim came from
A number of seconds is not the same as fast orientation. Complex ideas sometimes need more context; simple ideas need less.
Warning retention
A fixed intro duration is a false rule: the requirement is fast ORIENTATION, and complex ideas legitimately need more context while simple ideas need less.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the phrase carry INFORMATION about what is withheld, or is it a bare instruction? The store supplies its own resolving mechanism in aad4e27d043c (Joos): curiosity peaks at PARTIAL information — enough to guess, not enough to be certain — which is exactly why a contentless 'watch till the end' fails while a named, specific withheld item ('the bonus tip', 'the price') creates a live question. Restated: (a) name the withheld thing specifically enough to be guessable → works; (b) issue a bare instruction to stay → does nothing.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply at different channel sizes. The question that separates them:

What is the video's RUNTIME and format, and is the 60% figure a distribution gate or a descriptive correlate of a specific challenge-entertainment format at ~10-15 minutes? A 60% APV on a 12-minute challenge video and on a 52-minute build video are entirely different demands on the viewer. Restated: (a) within one channel at one roughly fixed length and format, a rising APV is a real improvement signal; (b) no APV number is a cross-channel or cross-length gate on distribution.

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the surface LOOP-SCORED (short-form, where completion and rewatch drive redistribution and the final second gates the loop) or watch-time-scored long-form? And is the trim removing a specifically DEAD trailing second, or removing runtime generally? Restated: (a) on short-form, trimming dead trailing frames is a direct lever on the loop metric; (b) on long-form, runtime is not the constraint — our own data has the longer half of the catalogue beating the shorter half on median first-28d views for 6 of 7 channels.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: No penalty is visible for a late top moment. Videos with the top peak after 60% (n=28): median APV 38.4%, median first-28d views 249,969. Videos with the top peak at or before 60% (n=61): median APV 38.7%, median first-28d views 221,408. Flagged peak positions overall are spread evenly across the runtime (p25 = 44%, median = 60%, p75 = 83%).

Caveat: This is the wrong shape of test for a claim about an intervention — comparing videos that HAPPEN to have a late peak against videos that happen to have an early one says nothing about what would happen if you moved content. Only an edit experiment can settle it. What the comparison does show is that a late top moment is not, by itself, a marker of a weaker video, which removes the diagnostic urgency the claim implies.

Where the claim came from
Its guidance suggests moving compelling content earlier when top moments occur late and creating new content by expanding top moments.

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: The data points the other way: rho(first-15s loss, first-28d views) is negative in 6/6 channels — Channel C -0.54, Channel D -0.45, Channel F -0.45, Channel E -0.37, Channel A -0.03, Channel G -0.04; pooled -0.32. Videos that got more views lost FEWER viewers in the opening. Median first-15s loss is also tightly clustered (6.5-9.4% across channels, worst single video 16.2%), so 'hockey stick' cliffs are rare in this set.

Caveat: Properly testing this needs CTR and impressions, which we do not hold — views conflate demand, delivery and click-rate, so a negative cliff-views correlation is not the same as a negative cliff-CTR correlation. The counter-signal is suggestive, not decisive. Note also that our channels simply may not produce the hockey-stick pathology: with a worst-case 16% first-15s loss, there may be no genuine instances of the phenomenon in the sample to diagnose.

Theory retention · earlier check spanned 6 channels Contested
Announcing the end of a video is what causes the terminal retention cliff - viewers leave the moment they perceive the core content is finished, so the transition to the next video must happen before any wrap-up signal.
Source: Sean Cannell
Contested — what would settle it

Which objective is being optimised — SESSION continuation (next-video click-through and watch time in this sitting) or REPEAT viewership (whether this viewer opens the channel's next upload)? These pull opposite ways at the outro, and each source is silently optimising a different one. The store's own 4214845e0b40 (Joos: under-delivering on a teased reward drives dopamine below baseline and suppresses willingness to wait in FUTURE videos) says the cost of the hand-off lands on later uploads, which is exactly the metric the retention curve cannot see. Restated: (a) optimising session watch time → hand off before the wrap-up signal; (b) optimising return rate on future uploads → resolve cleanly, and only then offer the next video. UNTESTABLE IN OUR DATA — we hold no next-video click-through or per-viewer return data.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: A terminal cliff is real and large in 6/6 channels. Final-10% loss (median): Channel G 35.3%, Channel C 28.1%, Channel D 23.0%, Channel F 22.4%, Channel E 14.1%, Channel A 9.4%. The matched mid-video 10% band loses far less: Channel C 1.1%, Channel F 3.0%, Channel G 2.2%, Channel E 2.0%, Channel D 10.6%, Channel A 9.2%. Per video, final-10% loss exceeds mid-10% loss in 97 of 119 cases. Median hazard by band is U-shaped: highest at 1-5%, ~0 through 46-90%, then rising again at 91-100%.

Caveat: The cliff exists; the stated CAUSE does not follow from it. We have no labelling of where a wrap-up signal occurs, so we cannot separate 'the creator announced the end' from the trivially expected fact that people stop watching when a video is over, from end-cards, from outros, or from the curve's own end artefact. The 3.7x spread between Channel A (9.4%) and Channel G (35.3%) shows the cliff size is not fixed, which is at least consistent with an editorial cause — but that is a hint, not a test.

Disputed

Opposite instructions for the same closing 20 seconds: suppress resolution and hand off to the next video, versus resolve cleanly and do not tease forward. Both are act-on-able and mutually exclusive.

Settle it by answering: Which objective is being optimised — SESSION continuation (next-video click-through and watch time in this sitting) or REPEAT viewership (whether this viewer opens the channel's next upload)? Restated: (a) optimising session watch time → hand off before the wrap-up signal; (b) optimising return rate on future uploads → resolve cleanly, and only then offer the next video. UNTESTABLE IN OUR DATA — we hold no next-video click-through or per-viewer return data.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: 42 flagged moments mention a sponsor; 32 of them (76%) are drops and 10 are peaks. So sponsor segments do disproportionately coincide with flagged losses in our cohort, and are not universally negative.

Caveat: This cannot test the claim's actual mechanism, which is about WHERE inside the read the brand name lands. We do not have per-read transcripts aligned to disclosure position, and 42 moments is thin. Worse, the sample is selection-biased in both directions: moments are surfaced only when the curve does something notable, so a sponsor read that held perfectly is invisible here, while a read placed near an unrelated drop gets credited with it. The 10 sponsor-adjacent PEAKS are worth noting against the assumption that ad reads always cost retention, but they are equally subject to that bias.

Checked: Naively the claim looks overwhelming: the first flagged drop is the largest in 99/99 videos, median hazard by order 15.3% -> -0.5% -> -1.0% -> -1.4%. But this is an artefact — the p25 of flagged drop positions is 1.0% of runtime, so 'first drop' is overwhelmingly 'the intro drop', which we already know is the biggest drop in 97% of videos. Excluding the first 10% of runtime leaves only 12 qualifying videos, and there the first post-intro drop is the largest in 6 of 12 — barely above chance, with median hazard by order 1.1% -> 0.0% -> -0.9%.

Caveat: Two blocking problems. (1) We have no ground-truth segment boundaries; flagged drops are our own model's output and are selected for being drops, which biases every comparison. (2) Once the intro is removed the usable sample collapses to 12 videos. This needs segment labelling before it can be judged.

Source: Derrel Eves
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the phrase carry INFORMATION about what is withheld, or is it a bare instruction? The store supplies its own resolving mechanism in aad4e27d043c (Joos): curiosity peaks at PARTIAL information — enough to guess, not enough to be certain — which is exactly why a contentless 'watch till the end' fails while a named, specific withheld item ('the bonus tip', 'the price') creates a live question. Restated: (a) name the withheld thing specifically enough to be guessable → works; (b) issue a bare instruction to stay → does nothing.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Where the claim came from
People are trying to click off a video as soon as you click on. And so that birthed optimized retention and you have to give people as many things to look at to prevent their brain switching off. But like having true retention is when you're consciously asking yourself, why does the audience want to stick around?
Theory retention
Returning viewers rising while new viewers stay flat or fall is a reach problem, not a loyalty problem: the channel is converting well but not being served to fresh audiences, and the fix is higher-TAM topics and packaging, not more community work.
Source: our own channel audits
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What did TOTAL views and impressions do over the same window? Flat new-viewer count with RISING totals is the accounting artefact of conversion (the cohort is being reclassified, not lost); flat new-viewer count with FLAT OR FALLING totals is a genuine reach ceiling. Restated: (a) new flat + total rising → benign, do not chase TAM; (b) new flat + total flat → reach ceiling, escalate topic TAM and packaging.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: The signature is pervasive and survives the duration control. rho(retention at 50%, first-28d views): Channel C -0.45 (partial -0.42), Channel D -0.51 (-0.50), Channel E -0.85 (-0.85), Channel A -0.47 (-0.42), Channel F -0.89 (-0.88); only Channel G is flat at +0.07 (+0.01). Intro loss points the same way: rho(1-10% loss, first-28d views) is POSITIVE in all 6 channels (+0.30 to +0.84) — the videos that shed the most of the room fastest are the videos that got the most views.

Caveat: This is the observation the claim predicts, but it is equally well explained by audience composition: a video that reaches a large cold browse/suggested audience necessarily loses more early and holds less throughout, with no promise-delivery failure anywhere. We cannot separate the two without traffic-source data, which we do not hold. And the claim's real content — that payoff debt is a DISTINCT failure from a weak idea — is not something a curve can adjudicate.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Channel C's titles are 30/30 implied ('This Chapter Is Finally Closing...', 'I'm Running Out of Options...', 'Addressing The Truth.') and she posts the BEST retention profile of all six analysed channels at every mark in the brief (76.7% at 30s, 43.9% at 50%, 35.1% at end). Within the channels that carry both kinds, implied beat explicit on retention at 50% in 3 of 4: Channel E 32.8% vs 28.1%, Channel A 38.6% vs 34.4%, Channel F 39.4% vs 37.0%; only Channel G reversed (36.8% vs 41.1%). In the corpus, explicit-objective titles score 1.08x vs 0.99x in maker-builds (n=31) but 0.79x vs 1.00x in roblox (n=9).

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. This refutes the NECESSITY wording ('must be legible in the title'), not the softer idea that explicit goals help some audiences. Title explicitness does not in fact separate our channels either way: Channel D is also 30/30 implied and posts the WORST retention profile of the six. The minority group is n=1-2 on three of the four within-channel splits. Confounded by niche, duration and audience.

The objective is the trackable goal that they are pursuing and it should be clear in the title and thumbnail. ... The why the why is the emotional part and most content on YouTube completely skips the why.

A rule that flags half to all of a channel's uploads as 'recut the opening' is not a rule that identifies anything.

Caveat: Front-loaded decay is a mechanical property of every retention curve — the click-bounce cohort leaves in the first 30 seconds no matter how good the opening is — so this test cannot separate 'the hook sits one segment late' from 'this is what all retention curves look like'. A real test needs an independent judgement of segment strength, which we do not have.

Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Bowls are common on maker channels — net recovery over 1pp in 97% of Channel C's videos, 100% of Morley's, 100% of Zac's, 78% of Channel E's, but only 47% of Channel D' and 30% of Channel A's. Inspection shows they are not exposition bowls: Channel C's 'I'm Running Out of Options...' falls 42%->23% between the 40% and 50% marks then recovers to 38% by 60%, and 31% of her non-intro flagged drops are attributed to sponsor reads. This is the V-shape our own segment work already documents — the read empties the room and skip-in traffic refills it.

Caveat: The claim's actual test (gap between an entity's first mention and its first on-screen use, correlated with 0-25% loss) requires full transcripts with entity timings, which we do not store. The bowl statistic is a max-minus-min over noisy data and is biased upward. What we can say is that the bowls we observe have a different, identified cause — not that front-loaded exposition never causes one.

Where the claim came from
When we see this, we let you want to think, hey, maybe I can put my exposition and spread it throughout the video. As a general rule of thumb, what we say is we only introduce information right before it becomes relevant. That's the retention rule.
Theory storytelling · earlier check spanned 6 channels
Because of the primacy effect, the first beat of a video sets how the whole video is perceived, so it must be the strongest emotional moment — which makes cold openings and any slow ease-in structurally bad.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: The associative half reproduces in 6/6 channels: rho(introLoss, end retention) = -0.79 Channel C, -0.24 Channel D, -0.63 Channel E, -0.52 Channel A, -0.27 Morley, -0.55 Zac. Videos that hold the opening hold the ending. But genuine peaks essentially never occur in the first decile (0% of 96 Channel C peaks, 0% of 85 Channel D, 0% of 33 Channel E, 3% of 36 Channel A); peak medians sit at 54%, 59%, 90% and 62% of duration. So on six healthy channels the strongest rewind-worthy moment is systematically NOT first.

Caveat: The correlation is almost certainly confounded by audience composition: a video pushed to a colder browse audience loses more early AND holds less throughout, which produces this pattern with no primacy effect at all. And the peak evidence cannot falsify the prescription — an opening that simply holds well produces no rewind spike, so absence of early peaks is not evidence of a weak opening. Causal claim, correlational data only.

Where the claim came from
Just make sure you set an exceptional tone. Strong emotion. That's what you're looking for here. So an impressive first thing. The first thing needs to set the tone for the rest of the video. No easing into it. No long... This is why cold openings tend to be very bad as well, typically, by the way.
Theory storytelling · earlier check spanned 6 channels
Ending a video by easing out lets the viewer emotionally calm down and undoes the peak-end benefit, so the final emotional beat should be held and the video cut off shortly after.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Which outcome is this video being built for — SESSION CONTINUATION or PROPAGATION? Joos's peak-end argument optimises the memory trace and the state the viewer is in when the next thumbnail appears: leave them elevated and they click. Eves and Gordon are optimising for what leaves the platform — the beat a viewer can retell, and the reflective residue that produces a comment. These are different currencies and a channel usually needs one more than the other. The second variable is whether the extra beat is a DECOMPRESSION (arousal decays — Joos is right) or a NEW small payoff (arousal is re-spiked before the cut — Eves's 'gush' is not an ease-out at all, which may dissolve half this conflict). We can measure the shape of the last 5% of the curve; we hold no shares or comment data, so the propagation half is untestable here.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Outros are expensive everywhere: median 95-100% hazard per 1% of video is 4.63% (Channel C), 3.49% (Channel D), 3.47% (Channel E), 3.89% (Morley), 5.47% (Zac), against 0.03-0.75% in the 60-90% band — the terminal band is the steepest post-intro band in 77-100% of videos on 5 of 6 channels. But the downstream half returns nothing: rho(end-hold_i, early-hold of next upload) = -0.21, -0.00, -0.02, -0.09, -0.35, -0.55 across 113 pairs, i.e. no benefit in the predicted direction.

Caveat: We cannot measure outro LENGTH, which is the actual variable — an abrupt cut and an extended wind-down both show up only as a terminal hazard number, and end cards inflate that number for every video regardless. The downstream null is the same test that refuted be6d7777d2f3 and shares its weakness: first-28d views and early retention on the next upload are dominated by packaging and distribution.

Where the claim came from
This is also the reason why you cannot, hey, this is the end segment, and then you ease out. You don't ease out, right? You don't ease out. Because then you allow the viewer to calm down. You don't allow them to calm down
Theory storytelling · earlier check spanned 6 channels
Outlining the video at the start is not bad for retention — a structure the audience can see makes them watch longer — which contradicts the common advice to get straight into content with no roadmap.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the front-loaded item NAVIGATION or PAYLOAD? A roadmap ('there are three attempts, the last one is the hard one') costs the viewer nothing to hold — it is a promise about order and it reduces the uncertainty that causes drift. A rule, a spec, a name, a constraint is payload: the viewer must retain it to understand a later beat, and they will not. So the repaired pair of rules is: front-load the SHAPE, never the CONTENT; anything the viewer must remember gets revealed at the moment it becomes load-bearing, with a visual. This is the cleanest scope repair in the store and it is entirely inside one source.

Checked: Per-second loss rate, 0-15s vs 15-30s vs 30-60s: Channel C 0.63% / 1.01% / 0.64%; Channel D 0.58% / 1.13% / 0.93%; Channel A 0.53% / 0.87% / 0.41%; Channel F 0.51% / 1.05% / 0.81%; Channel G 0.56% / 1.40% / 0.64%. Cross-cutting, for those who don't know that, is simply where you take five seconds from your A story, five seconds from your B story, five seconds from your A story, five seconds from your B story. Theory storytelling
Information given verbally in the intro is forgotten by the time it matters unless it is shown visually again later, so rules and setup must be revealed one at a time as they are used ('highlight rule, show rule'), not listed up front.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the front-loaded item NAVIGATION or PAYLOAD? A roadmap ('there are three attempts, the last one is the hard one') costs the viewer nothing to hold — it is a promise about order and it reduces the uncertainty that causes drift. A rule, a spec, a name, a constraint is payload: the viewer must retain it to understand a later beat, and they will not. So the repaired pair of rules is: front-load the SHAPE, never the CONTENT; anything the viewer must remember gets revealed at the moment it becomes load-bearing, with a visual. This is the cleanest scope repair in the store and it is entirely inside one source.

Where the claim came from
in terms of structural storytelling, the Dan Harmon Story Circle is what I find a lot of creators talking about... if you just Google Dan Harmon Story Circle, you can find, like, the exact beats to what any episode of television typically follows.
Theory storytelling
Front-loading a protagonist's motivating backstory rather than distributing it through the piece makes the audience like them — Pixar cut Finding Nemo's dispersed flashbacks to the opening specifically because test viewers did not like Marlin.
Source: Jonathan Hurwitz (10 years at Disney/Pixar)
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Has the audience already COMMITTED to finishing? Joos names the discriminator himself in 4ad699f1dd60: the YouTube intro's job is context and the rules of the world, not character exposition, 'because viewers arrive without any commitment to finish, unlike film audiences.' A cinema audience has paid and cannot leave, so early backstory is an investment; a YouTube viewer is auditing and early backstory is an unpaid bill. The second variable is what the backstory is FOR — Pixar needed the viewer to LIKE a character they would spend 100 minutes with; a YouTube creator's 'why I'm doing this' is usually a justification the viewer has not yet asked for. Our own data locates the exact edge: median retention at 15s is 91.9-94.2% across all six analysed channels but falls to 72-79% by 30s (Channel E excepted at 93.5%). The first 15 seconds are nearly free; the bill lands between 15s and 60s. That is direct support for our strategist's 353818aee0a4 placement of the emotional WHY at 15-20s — after the free window, before the cliff.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: The two metrics name a different worst moment (more than 2 percentage-points apart in position) in 33 of 119 videos — 28%. When they disagree the relative metric picks a LATER moment in 32 of those 33 cases (27% of all videos). Median worst-moment position: 48% of the video under percentage points, 67% under the relative measure — a systematic late shift, exactly the underweighting the claim describes.

Caveat: Partly arithmetic: dividing by a shrinking denominator must push attention later, so this confirms the mechanism rather than discovering it. What it does NOT establish is that the relative measure identifies the more IMPORTANT moment — that would need an outcome to validate against (a fix that worked), which we do not have. Note the team's own pipeline ranks by excess viewers lost rather than by ratio alone, precisely because a pure ratio over-rewards small absolute losses late in a video; the claim as stated does not carry that correction.

we never look at the percentage but we do sometimes use the relative drops as a measurement of impact so at the beginning we see that 100% to 80% is 20% drop well 50% to 40% is also 20% drop that's relative retention ... Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: rho(duration, AVD) is +0.69 to +0.85 in 6/6 channels (pooled +0.80) — the baseline effect is real and large. rho(duration, APV) is negative in 5/6. Of 65 qualifying shorter-beats-longer-on-AVD pairs across 5 channels (Channel C 19, Channel D 16, Channel A 25, Channel E 4, Channel F 1; Channel G had 0), the shorter video ALSO had the higher APV in 65/65 — 100%.

Caveat: The 65/65 result is close to arithmetically forced: AVD = APV x duration, so a shorter video with higher AVD must have a higher APV once the duration gap exceeds the AVD gap. That makes the inference SOUND rather than empirically surprising — which is exactly what the claim asserts, so it counts, but nobody should read 100% as an independent finding. The 20% duration-gap threshold is my choice; a smaller gap would admit near-ties.

A high, flat retention chart is evidence of NARROW appeal only when impressions or views on that video are also low — it then suggests YouTube did not judge the video broadly appealing enough to push. High retention and wide appeal do genuinely co-occur, so the chart alone cannot carry the diagnosis; it needs impression and view context first.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the comparison WITHIN one video (same audience composition, before-vs-after an edit) or ACROSS videos in a catalogue (audience width varying)? Eves is asserting a counterfactual on a fixed audience; Joos is describing a cross-sectional correlation in which audience breadth is the confounder and dominates. Restated conditionally: (a) holding reach constant, later 50%-departure raises AVD and is worth editing for; (b) across a channel's catalogue, retention-at-50% is a proxy for audience narrowness and predicts FEWER views, so it must never be used as a cross-video ranking of quality.

Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so its Law standing rests on a human sign-off and earlier manual checks, NOT on the measurement ledger. Treat it as the team's settled judgement rather than a measured result. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Supported: The opposite holds in 6/6 channels — the highest-APV videos are systematically the LOWER-view ones (pooled rho -0.54). Concretely, Channel A's most-retentive video ('IT ACTUALLY WORKED!', APV 54.0%) drew 212k 28d views against a channel median of 224k, while its top-view videos sit at 21-27% APV.

Caveat: We observe the association, not the algorithmic reasoning behind it. 'YouTube did not think it was broadly appealing' is an unobservable claim about ranking internals; the data is equally consistent with narrow topics simply attracting a self-selected audience that watches longer. Do not read this as 'high retention is bad' — read it as 'retention rank is not a proxy for reach rank'.

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. Strong selection confound: creators choose length to fit the material, so a big ambitious build gets both more minutes and more interest. The corpus test — which removes channel-size effects — finds essentially NOTHING (rho +0.10 / +0.04 / -0.08), which is the honest reading: length is not a penalty, but it is also not a lever. The claim's own evidence ('longest curves were disproportionately high-view') is exactly the confounded within-channel version.
