Warning analytics · earlier check spanned 6 channels
A one-sample uptick in the curve is usually a mid-roll YouTube ad causing viewers to rewind for lost context, not genuine rewatch interest — a real spike must persist across multiple data points, and single-point ticks should be ignored entirely.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)
Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — so it stays a Warning on the strength of practitioner testimony. A failure mode is worth avoiding on good authority; it has simply never been put to our arithmetic. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Of 2,196 qualifying rises, 1,259 (57%) persist two samples later and 937 (43%) fade. So single-sample ticks are a minority of rises, not the usual case, and a blanket 'ignore single-point ticks entirely' would discard 43% of all upward movement in these curves.

Caveat: The core of the claim is untestable here: we hold no ad-break placement data, so we cannot attribute ANY tick to a mid-roll. The persistence rule the claim recommends is already implemented in this codebase's retention analysis (a rise counts as a replay peak only if it survives the next sample and no comparable drop precedes it), so the prescription is not neutral evidence — our curves have been shaped by the very filter being evaluated. My 0.2pp and two-sample thresholds are also arbitrary; different cuts move the 57/43 split.

Where the claim came from
often when you see a tick like this, I want you to check for a YouTube ad. ... it's not because it necessarily negatively impacts retention, but simply because people skip back and that causes this uptick. ... So when we do this one, no solution needed. If you see these things, don't even act upon it.
Warning analytics
Viral reach can be an anti-signal: a video may attract a large but incompatible audience that never continues into the channel, so success must be measured by follow-on viewing, returning behaviour, and comment language rather than views.
Source: idea-engine research dossier

Warning analytics Contested
Judging a video by its first 24 hours is actively deceptive, because different videos require different numbers of impressions before the SAME viewer clicks — one video converts on the second showing, another on the fifth.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)
Contested — what would settle it

Is day-one CTR read as an ABSOLUTE number or as a residual against the SAME channel's own prior day-one CTRs, and is that channel's day-one audience compositionally stable? Paddy's claim is scoped to established channels, where day one is a near-constant subscriber-heavy panel — that stability is what makes the comparison legitimate. Joos's counterexample is impression-accumulation rate varying per video, which corrupts absolute readings. Note the store already carries a partial carve-out from Joos himself (4f18d60d2b00: on news and patch-update channels day-one behaviour genuinely does carry signal). UNTESTABLE IN OUR DATA — we hold no CTR or impressions at all.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: No relationship: rho(cluster supply, cluster median outlier) = -0.02 across 53 clusters. If anything supply runs the other way — high-supply clusters (15+ videos, n=6) have a median outlier of 1.17x against 1.02x for low-supply clusters (5-7 videos, n=35). The largest cluster, 'animal hospital' (49 videos), medians 1.28x; 'meccha chameleon' (22 videos) medians 1.21x. Only 'motorcycle camping' (24 videos, 0.89x) fits the claim.

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. The proxy is crude and this verdict should not be over-read. Bigram clusters are not 'materially similar versions', and I could not impose the claim's 90-day recency restriction — the corpus spans years of publish dates. Crowded subjects here are crowded because they WORK (a popular Roblox game attracts both supply and demand), so supply and demand are entangled in a way this test cannot separate. Read this as: our data gives no support for a supply penalty, not as proof that saturation never hurts.

Where the claim came from
Separate reachable demand from total popularity. Count recent qualified videos, their normalized performance, and how many materially similar versions already exist.
Theory analytics · earlier check spanned 53 channels
A smaller absolute view count on a small channel can be stronger demand evidence than a much larger count on a big channel: a 10x-over-baseline video carries more information than a 1.1x-over-baseline video with 10x the raw views.
Source: idea-engine research dossier

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Absolute views and outlier score are only weakly related (rho +0.28), and channel size is orthogonal to outlier magnitude (rho(channel median views, outlier score) = -0.03) — so a big channel does not manufacture big outlier scores. Of the top decile by ABSOLUTE views (n=112, all above 2.31M views), 64% score below 1.5x on their own channel. Conversely, of the 62 videos at 3x+ their own baseline, 39% have below-corpus-median absolute views.

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. This establishes that the two rankings are largely independent — it does NOT establish that the normalised one is better DEMAND evidence, which is the claim's actual assertion. Testing that would require following a topic from a small-channel breakout to a later large-channel attempt, which we have no data for. The corpus is peer/trending/search collected, so channels are not a random sample and outlier scores rest on however many videos we happened to collect per channel (median well under 30).

Where the claim came from
A 100,000-view upload on a channel normally earning 10,000 may be more informative than a 1,000,000-view upload on a channel normally earning 900,000.

Among matched pairs the surviving view gap is large: Channel C 69 pairs, median 1.26x and up to 2.0x; Channel D 34 pairs, median 1.54x, up to 4.7x; Channel G 9 pairs, median 1.67x; Channel E 6 pairs, median 3.58x, up to 17.6x.

We hold no CTR, no impressions, and no traffic-source split, so topic demand, seasonality, algorithmic timing and subject breadth are all folded into that residual alongside packaging. Treat the pattern as 'watchability did not cause the gap' — not as 'packaging did'.

Theory analytics · earlier check spanned 6 channels Contested
A video with high retention but low views has a PACKAGING problem, not a content problem — the retention proves the video can hold a wider audience than the packaging reached, so it is the prime repackaging candidate.
Source: internal strategy session
Contested — what would settle it

Is the video's retention high in ABSOLUTE terms, or high as a RESIDUAL — above what the channel's own retention-versus-views relationship predicts at that view count? Only the residual carries information; the absolute number is confounded by exactly the mechanism claim B names. OUR DATA SETTLES THIS: rank correlation between retention-at-50% and first-28d views is -0.45 (Channel C), -0.51 (Channel D), -0.85 (Channel E), -0.47 (Channel A), -0.89 (Channel F), +0.07 (Channel G) — negative on 5 of 6 channels, strongly so on the two small-n maker channels. The repackaging rule must therefore be re-specified as 'retention above the channel's fitted expectation at that view count', and the existing verdict table in our own pipeline should be checked against this.

Checked: The quadrant is the DEFAULT, not a diagnosis: among below-median-view videos, the share that also sit above median APV is Channel C 60%, Channel D 60%, Channel A 73%, Channel F 80%, Channel G 80%, Channel E 100%. This is forced by the underlying negative views/retention correlation (pooled -0.54) — low-view videos are ALSO the high-retention ones almost by construction, so the rule flags 60-100% of every channel's underperformers and discriminates almost nothing.

Caveat: Two separate problems. First, no repackage outcomes exist in our data, so the causal claim ('retention proves it can hold a wider audience') is untestable — retention was measured on the narrow audience it actually reached, and there is no evidence it would survive a wider one; the negative views/retention correlation is direct evidence against exactly that extrapolation. Second, even as a screening heuristic the rule barely narrows the field. The team's existing 'repackage or double down' verdict table, which ranks retention-at-50% AGAINST first-28d views rather than thresholding both, is the sounder version of this idea.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What did TOTAL views and impressions do over the same window? Flat new-viewer count with RISING totals is the accounting artefact of conversion (the cohort is being reclassified, not lost); flat new-viewer count with FLAT OR FALLING totals is a genuine reach ceiling. Restated: (a) new flat + total rising → benign, do not chase TAM; (b) new flat + total flat → reach ceiling, escalate topic TAM and packaging.

Law strategy · earlier check spanned 6 channels
Watchability is rarely the binding constraint on a channel; clickability usually is. If nobody clicks, nothing else can happen, so the default diagnosis for a stalled channel is ideation and packaging before retention.
Source: our own channel audits
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply at different channel sizes. The question that separates them:

Is the channel already being SERVED impressions it is failing to convert, or is it not being served at all? Retention work can only compound if distribution already exists to be amplified — Joos's channel was at 17M monthly views when he started, i.e. YouTube was already handing it audience. The audits' channels are at 54k-988k median first-28d views, where the gap is upstream. Our own data settles the video-level half of this: rank correlation between retention-at-50% and first-28d views is NEGATIVE on five of six channels (Channel C -0.45, Channel D -0.51, Channel E -0.85, Channel A -0.47, Channel F -0.89; Channel G 0.07). Within a channel, the videos that reached furthest retained WORSE — because reach recruits non-core viewers who leave earlier. So 'improve retention' is not a lever on views at the video level; it is at best a channel-level lever operating through a distribution regime our data does not cover. The discriminating question is the traffic-source mix, which we do not hold.

Supported: spearman(hazard SD, normalised views) is POSITIVE on 5 of 6 channels — Channel C +0.53, Channel D +0.53, Channel E +0.62, Channel A +0.30, Channel F +0.72, Channel G -0.35. spearman(retention level, normalised views) is NEGATIVE on 6 of 6: -0.51, -0.48, -0.85, -0.47, -0.79, -0.66. The flat-and-high quadrant underperforms its channel on 6 of 6: Channel C 0.93x vs 1.16x rest, Channel D 0.89 vs 1.21, Channel E 0.73 vs 1.38, Channel A 0.96 vs 1.20, Channel F 0.79 vs 1.79, Channel G 0.93 vs 1.07. This is the same quadrant the brief's negative retention-vs-views correlations point at (-0.45 to -0.89 on five channels).

Caveat: Reverse causation is the live alternative and I cannot rule it out: a video that reaches beyond the core necessarily collects casual viewers who leave early, which mechanically produces both a lower level and a lumpier curve. So the data cannot show that a flat curve CAUSES limited reach — only that flat-and-high co-occurs with low reach. The actionable half survives either reading: a flat high curve is not evidence of a healthy video, and retention edits are the wrong lever for it. Within-channel correlations over 9-30 videos are weak individually; the strength here is that the sign is identical on 6 independent channels across 3 niches.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: spearman(gap CV, median views): maker-builds -0.44 (n=12), motorcycle -0.67 (n=14), roblox +0.19 (n=16), pooled -0.36 (n=42). So irregular cadence is associated with fewer views in two niches and slightly more in the third. Within channels, the gap preceding a video predicts nothing about that video's first-28d views (pooled spearman 0.00, n=113).

Caveat: Gap CV is contaminated by hiatus-and-decline: a channel that is dying uploads erratically, so the negative correlation may be an effect of decline rather than a cause. Without traffic-source splits the claim's actual conditional cannot be evaluated at all — this is the half of the test that would matter.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the audience's attachment to the PERSON or to the CONTENT CONTRACT — and does the variety span different subjects inside one relationship, or different viewer JOBS (entertain me vs teach me vs let me follow you) on one feed? Hayden's mechanism is tier conflict: a superfan deep-dive and a broad-appeal video ask a viewer to be two different people. our strategist's 0c8258f3e010 names the other regime — when attachment is to the person, escalation and strictness stop being required. The store's own related claim (7563e845b615 aside) also warns of a measurement trap: 7a816d0ac0e5 says preference for an aesthetic is not a prediction of watch behaviour, so '40% said they want variety' is a stated preference and the behavioural test is whether the mixed uploads on that channel actually held their returning share.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: 8 slowdown events found. Duration moved up in 4 (Stuff Made Here 17→24min, William Osman 14→18min, TwoWheelObsession 9→11min, Blacktail-class cases), down in 3 (April Wilkerson 10→8min, Motovudu 11→7min, Channel B 14→10min), flat in 1 — so slowing down was NOT generally accompanied by an obvious production increase, which is consistent with the claim's warning. Median views fell in 6 of 8 (e.g. Stuff Made Here 13.50M→6.51M, I did a thing 5.47M→3.91M, BriannaPlayz 281,539→167,104).

Caveat: The view comparison is unusable as evidence: the split is chronological and views are lifetime, so the 'before' window is always the older one and mechanically accumulates more views. Duration and title length are thin proxies for 'substantive change' — they cannot see extra shoot days, better writing, or a new set. Treat only the duration observation as data, and even that at n=8.

he was like, I'm going to increase the quality. I'm like, okay, what has changed? Nothing has changed. You just upload less. ... Now, after a few times doing it now, he's actually changed, right? A trend does not automatically fit a channel's audience, and viral views are not proof of the right audience — the test is follow-on viewing, returning behaviour and comment language, not the view count.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What is this Short being scored on — views on the Shorts feed, or qualified arrivals at the long-form catalogue? Hopper is measuring the Short as a product competing against native short-form, where a repurposed clip loses on comparison. our strategist is measuring it as a funnel, where the Short's job is to make a subscriber who recognises the channel when they arrive — a native Short that wins the feed but misrepresents the catalogue produces exactly the ghost subscriber, which is Thomas Brag's 6e81c9f8f955 mis-classification problem in miniature. Both are true once the metric is named: extract the SUBJECT from long-form, re-cut the GRAMMAR for vertical. The genuinely unresolved part is whether an extracted-subject Short can be made native enough to also win on reach.

But what we've discovered now is there's so many creators who are creating specifically for TikTok or specifically for Instagram Reels, specifically for YouTube shorts, specifically for LinkedIn. You know, like, they're just creating content just for that.
Warning strategy
An audience assembled around a format or gimmick is transactional and churns when the format ages; an audience assembled around a stated value survives format changes, so format-dependence is a longevity risk.
Source: CreatorNow
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the channel's growth currently coming from NEW algorithmic reach or from an existing audience returning — and what is the audience actually attached to? Eves's mechanism is a classifier problem (a machine needs a repeated pattern to find lookalike viewers) and only binds while the channel still needs to be discovered. Kandil's mechanism is a churn problem and only binds once an audience exists that can leave. The two truths are sequential, not opposed: hold the format while the algorithm is still learning who you are; build a stated value on top of it before the format ages. The test for which regime you are in is whether returning-viewer share is still climbing or has plateaued.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What is this Short being scored on — views on the Shorts feed, or qualified arrivals at the long-form catalogue? Hopper is measuring the Short as a product competing against native short-form, where a repurposed clip loses on comparison. our strategist is measuring it as a funnel, where the Short's job is to make a subscriber who recognises the channel when they arrive — a native Short that wins the feed but misrepresents the catalogue produces exactly the ghost subscriber, which is Thomas Brag's 6e81c9f8f955 mis-classification problem in miniature. Both are true once the metric is named: extract the SUBJECT from long-form, re-cut the GRAMMAR for vertical. The genuinely unresolved part is whether an extracted-subject Short can be made native enough to also win on reach.

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Across 46 channels and 1,290 videos: 76 within-channel format families reach 2+ uses, 15 reach 4+, only 3 reach 10+, and ZERO reach 20 (largest run = 14). Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: First entrant median residual +0.138 vs later +0.054, MW p=0.040 (28 clusters, 20 channels) — direction matches the claim. But the decay the claim predicts is absent: among later entrants, spearman(entry order, performance) = +0.05 (n=100), and per-cluster the median correlation is -0.22 with a 9-negative/5-positive split across 14 clusters, i.e. noise.

Caveat: The first-mover premium is confounded by selection — clusters form around a video that already succeeded, so being first is correlated with being a hit by construction. We cannot observe commissioning date or a subject's view velocity at commissioning time, which is what the claim is actually about; the daily niche crawl has not run long enough to give velocity histories. This is a correlational step function, not evidence of a timing mechanism.

Theory strategy · earlier check spanned 13 channels
A channel should retire its signature device BEFORE performance declines, because the decline is caused by accumulated exposure, not by the device becoming worse.
Source: Alan Garnett
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the device a RECOGNITION marker or a NOVELTY device — and is the repetition within one video or across many? Two separate scopes are collapsed here. (1) Within a video, repetition is dead time the viewer has already paid for; across videos, the same repetition is what makes the channel identifiable in a feed. Joos's own two claims resolve on exactly that axis. (2) A device whose effect is RECOGNITION (a font, a set, a returning theme) does not fatigue — Gannett's own 180d93548c26 exempts habit-forming products from the exposure curve. A device whose effect depends on SURPRISE (a running gag, an escalating stunt, a signature reveal) does fatigue, and Gannett's retire-early rule applies only to it. The operational test: if removing it would make a regular viewer fail to recognise the channel, it is recognition — hold it. If removing it would make them notice nothing, it was novelty and is already spent. Gannett's b9b71a3fb0a1 adds the timing guard: core-audience boredom arrives before mainstream discovery, so core complaints are not the retirement signal.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Median spearman(repetition index, age-adjusted performance) = -0.20, with 9 families negative and 5 positive. Early half of a run: median residual -0.007 (n=42); later half -0.074 (n=46); Mann-Whitney p=0.144. The unadjusted number is -0.34, but that is inflated by video age and should not be quoted.

Caveat: Directionally consistent with exposure fatigue but not significant, and badly underpowered — 15 families is not enough to separate fatigue from the ordinary decline of any channel's mid-list ideas. Title-signature families are a coarse stand-in for a 'signature device' (a recurring segment, catchphrase or editing motif is invisible in a title). The claim's actionable half — that retiring EARLY beats retiring on decline — needs cases of deliberate retirement, which we cannot identify at all.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Which surface is this channel's long-form distribution actually coming from, and what is the GAP between the two uploads? The cannibalisation mechanism is freshness ranking within a single channel's slot on the subscriber home feed — it binds hard on a channel whose long-form views are subscriber-fed and barely at all on one fed by suggested/search. The second missing variable is time: 'the day after' is not the same decision as 'four days later'. Reframe both as one conditional: if long-form is home-feed-fed, Shorts are cadence-fillers only in the trough between uploads, never inside the freshness window; if it is suggested-fed, the medium genuinely does not compete. We cannot test this — traffic-source splits are not exposed by the API we use.

Source: our own channel audits
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is this an EPISODE or a TENTPOLE? Hurwitz's 5cb5e965b040 already draws the line: regular uploads are episodes of an open-ended series, tentpoles are finite films, and the two require different structures. An episodic container has slack — the metric can legitimately set the dial because the format can absorb another segment. A tentpole's length is determined by its payoff, and cutting to hit a number breaks the thing people came for. Our own data supports the audits' direction within episodic catalogues: the longer half of the catalogue won on median first-28d views for six of seven channels (Channel C 321,662 vs 291,465; Channel D 65,205 vs 48,143; Channel A 251,961 vs 218,645; Channel F 1,012,676 vs 963,861; Channel B 287,063 vs 207,873; Channel G 485,039 vs 367,785). The single exception is Channel E — the channel with by far the longest median duration at 52 minutes — where longer LOST (691,316 vs 863,878). That is the shape of a permission-to-lengthen rule with a channel-specific ceiling, not a universal one, and it is why the rule must be re-read each quarter rather than applied once.

Where the claim came from

Theory strategy
Channel growth should be read as a staircase, not a ramp: acquire new viewers, then learn to convert them, then acquire again — high returning share secures baseline views while high new share is what produces outliers, and the two should alternate rather than be optimised simultaneously.
Source: our own channel audits

Theory strategy
Both familiarity and novelty are required for interest, but they should be split by layer: keep fonts, graphics, pacing, recurring characters, sets and returning music consistent across videos, and put the novelty into the content itself.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the device a RECOGNITION marker or a NOVELTY device — and is the repetition within one video or across many? Two separate scopes are collapsed here. (1) Within a video, repetition is dead time the viewer has already paid for; across videos, the same repetition is what makes the channel identifiable in a feed. Joos's own two claims resolve on exactly that axis. (2) A device whose effect is RECOGNITION (a font, a set, a returning theme) does not fatigue — Gannett's own 180d93548c26 exempts habit-forming products from the exposure curve. A device whose effect depends on SURPRISE (a running gag, an escalating stunt, a signature reveal) does fatigue, and Gannett's retire-early rule applies only to it. The operational test: if removing it would make a regular viewer fail to recognise the channel, it is recognition — hold it. If removing it would make them notice nothing, it was novelty and is already spent. Gannett's b9b71a3fb0a1 adds the timing guard: core-audience boredom arrives before mainstream discovery, so core complaints are not the retirement signal.

Source: Yes Theory
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the audience being asked to GENERATE the next idea or to DIAGNOSE their own existing relationship with the channel? Viewers cannot name a video that does not exist — that is the faster-horses failure and Brag is right about it. But viewers are the only available authority on why they came back, which is a report on their own behaviour, not a forecast. The second discriminator is stated vs revealed: the ideation packet's 7a816d0ac0e5 and Derral Eves's 4cb454d7fdc9 both warn that a stated preference (and feedback from outside the demographic) does not predict watch behaviour and can corrupt early signal. So: ask about attachment and about defects in things they already watched (Treadaway's f7449da8bdd2 — fixing the named complaint measurably improved the sequel); never ask for the concept.

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — which is exactly why it sits at Theory rather than higher — the rung means the cause and effect behind it has not been quantified. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Where the claim came from
The answer, it turned out, was neither the best possible placement the researchers concluded, was to be somewhere in the middle. That is to say, between the establishment and the fringe.
